## Abstract

We prove relative Langlands duality for $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ . These symmetric spaces arise in the setting of the linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet when $p=q$ , and exhibit non-tempered behavior when $q>p+1$ . Via the real-symmetric correspondence, we establish a derived Satake equivalence for the real group $G_{\mathbf{R}}=U(p,q)$ , and use it to obtain a constructible realization of coherent sheaves on Kato’s exotic nilpotent cones. Along the way, we describe the dual variety of $X$ in terms of the Whittaker cotangent bundle and regular centralizers, viewed as Coulomb branches.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Relative Langlands duality

The relative Langlands program of Ben-Zvi, Sakellaridis and Venkatesh [BZSV] proposes geometric mechanisms for observed and conjectural relations between periods and L-functions.

A fundamental conjecture in the program predicts that given a complex reductive group $G$ , with dual group $\check{G}$ , and a homogeneous spherical $G$ -variety $X$ , there exists a (graded) Hamiltonian $\check{G}$ -variety $\check{M}$ with moment map $\mu:\check{M}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ equipped with a commuting $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -action satisfying $\mu(t\cdot m)=t^{2}\mu(m)$ , and a relative derived Satake equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{M})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash} $$

On the left or automorphic side, $\mathfrak{L}X$ is the formal loop space of $X$ , $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ is the formal arc space of $G$ , and $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ is the bounded constructible dg-derived category of $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -equivariant sheaves on $\mathfrak{L}X$ . On the right or spectral/Galois side, $\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{M})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash}$ is the sheared dg-category of $\check{G}$ -equivariant perfect dg-modules over the ring of functions on $\check{M}$ viewed as a dg-algebra with trivial differential and grading given by the $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -action. The shearing notation and the shifted vector spaces used below are defined in Section 4.2; the parity convention is specified in Section 4.4.

Moreover, the relative derived Satake equivalence (1) should be compatible with the natural monoidal actions under the derived Satake equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}[2]) $$

where $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}=\mathfrak{L}G/\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ is the affine Grassmannian, $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})$ acts on $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ by convolution, and $\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}[2])$ acts on $\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{M})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash}$ by tensor product through $\mu$ .

### 1.2. Linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet

An important instance of relative duality is the linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet [FJ]: here one takes $G=GL_{2p}$ , so with dual group $\check{G}=GL_{2p}$ , and studies $X=GL_{2p}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{p})$ with expected dual

$$ \check{M}=GL_{2p}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[1]) $$

$$ \check{M}/\check{G}=(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[1])/\mathrm{Sp}_{2p} $$

Similar phenomena can be observed more generally, when one takes $G=GL_{p+q}$ , $q\geq p$ , so with dual group $\check{G}=GL_{p+q}$ , and studies $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ with expected dual

$$ \check{M}=GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}^{*}_{q-p}[2]\sslash GL_{q-p}) $$

$$ \check{M}/\check{G}=(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}^{*}_{q-p}[2]\sslash GL_{q-p})/\mathrm{Sp}_{2p} $$

In the associated-bundle presentation the grading also acts on the group factor by $g\mapsto g\lambda(t)^{-1}$ , with $\lambda$ as in (8); after quotienting by $\check{G}$ , only the displayed fiber degrees remain. When $p=q$ , the final $GL_{q-p}$ quotient factor is a point. Note this is tempered if and only if $q=p$ or $q=p+1$ .

Our main result is a relative derived Satake equivalence in this setting:

#### Theorem 1.2.1.

(see Theorem 4.2.1) For $G=GL_{p+q}$ , $q\geq p$ , and $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ , there is a relative derived Satake equivalence of dg-categories

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}^{*}_{q-p}[2]\sslash GL_{q-p}) $$

compatible with the natural monoidal actions under the derived Satake equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}[2]) $$

Within the above derived Satake equivalence, we also find an abelian equivalence. According to [CN, Section 8.4], the category $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}^{b}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ admits a perverse $t$ -structure. We denote the corresponding category of perverse sheaves by $\mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ .

#### Theorem 1.2.2.

(see Theorem 4.4.1) There is an equivalence of abelian category

$$ \mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\cong\begin{cases}\wedge^{*}(T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p})\mathrm{-mod}(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}))\ \ \ \ \ p=q,\\
\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p})\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ p\neq q.\end{cases} $$

### 1.3. Derived Satake equivalence for $U(p,q)$

A key feature of the linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet, and more generally of $G=GL_{p+q}$ acting on $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ is that $X$ is a symmetric space, i.e. $K=GL_{p}\times GL_{q}$ is the fixed-points of an involution $\theta$ of $G$ . Among many consequences, this allows one to reinterpret the relative derived Satake equivalence of Theorem 1.2.1 in terms of the unitary group $G_{\mathbf{R}}=U(p,q)$ , which is quasi-split if and only if $q=p$ or $q=p+1$ . Following [CN] and recalled as Proposition 2.4.5 below, the automorphic side admits a natural equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\cong D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)}) $$

where $\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)}=\mathfrak{L}U(p,q)/\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)$ is the real affine Grassmannian of $U(p,q)$ . Moreover, the equivalence (2) is compatible with natural actions of the derived Satake category.

So the relative derived Satake equivalence of Theorem 1.2.1 can be restated as a real derived Satake equivalence:

#### Theorem 1.3.1 (see Theorem 4.2.1).

For $G_{\mathbf{R}}=U(p,q)$ there is a real derived Satake equivalence of dg-categories

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}^{*}_{q-p}[2]\sslash GL_{q-p}) $$

compatible with the natural monoidal actions under the derived Satake equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}[2]) $$

According to [N], there is natural perverse $t$ -structure on $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})$ and we denote by $\mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})$ the corresponding category of perverse sheaves.

#### Theorem 1.3.2.

(see Theorem 4.4.1) There is an equivalence of abelian category

$$ \mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\cong\begin{cases}\wedge^{*}(T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p})\mathrm{-mod}(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}))\ \ \ \ \ p=q,\\
\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p})\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ p\neq q.\end{cases} $$

### 1.4. Whittaker cotangent bundles and regular centralizers

Another key feature of the linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet, and more generally of $G=GL_{p+q}$ acting on $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ is that $K=GL_{p}\times GL_{q}$ is a Levi subgroup of $G$ . The work of the third author [M] suggests the alternative description of the dual variety $\check{M}$ as the affine closure of the Whittaker cotangent bundle

$$ \check{M}\cong\overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})} $$

here $T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})$ is the Hamiltonian reduction of $T^{*}\check{G}$ by a maximal unipotent subgroup $\check{U}=[\check{B},\check{B}]\subset\check{G}$ at $-d\psi_{\check{K}}$ for the right action $g\mapsto gu^{-1}$ , where $\psi_{\check{K}}:\check{U}\to\mathbb{G}_{a}$ is an additive character nontrivial precisely on the simple roots of the dual Levi $\check{K}=GL_{p}\times GL_{q}$ (see Section 3.4 for more details).

On the other hand, a recent general result of Ginzburg [Gi] suggests another description of the dual variety in terms of regular centerlizers group schemes:

$$ \check{M}\cong\overline{\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}}/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}} $$

here the right hand side is the affine closure of the quotient $\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}}/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}$ , where $J_{\check{G}}\to\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}}$ , $J_{\check{K}}\to\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}$ are the group schemes of regular centralizers, and $\pi:\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}\to\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}}$ is the natural projection (see Section 3.5 for more details).

Indeed, we prove the isomorphisms (3) and (4), which is the key step in our approach to Relative Langlands duality for linear periods:

#### Theorem 1.4.1 (see Theorem 3.6.1).

There are $\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -equivariant isomorphisms of affine varieties over $\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ in the following commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{\overline{\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}}/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\simeq} \scriptstyle{\simeq} \textstyle{\overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\check{M}} $$

In fact, the isomorphism $\overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})}\cong\overline{(\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}$ in Theorem 1.4.1 follows from the work in [Ga, M], which is valid when $\check{K}$ is a general Levi subgroups (not necessarily symmetric or spherical), and the main step in the proof is the isomorphism (3). The proof uses a generalization of Kostant theorem, see Section 3.7, and a Lagrangian correspondence between $T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})$ and $\check{M}$ , see Section 27.

Since $\check{M}$ is smooth, as a corollary of the theorem we obtain the following:

#### Corollary 1.4.2 (see Corollary 3.6.2).

The affine closures $\overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})}\cong\overline{(\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}$ are smooth.

#### Remark 1.4.3.

It is proved in [Gi, Corollary 3.1.6] that the affine closure $\overline{\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}}/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}$ for general connected reductive subgroup $\check{K}\subset\check{G}$ is an irreducible normal variety. However, the smoothness of the affine closures in setting of Levi symmetric subgroup $\check{K}=\mathrm{GL}_{p}\times\mathrm{GL}_{q}$ was unexpected at least by the authors.

### 1.5. Exotic nilpotent cones

Finally, this paper also makes contact with the exotic nilpotent cones of [Ka]. Recall the dual variety

$$ \check{M}/\check{G}=(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}^{*}_{q-p}[2]\sslash GL_{q-p})/\mathrm{Sp}_{2p} $$

The null-cone for the $\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}$ action on $\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]$ , denoted by

$$ \mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}^{\prime}\subset\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1] $$

is known as the exotic nilpotent cones of [Ka]. Consider the dg category $D^{b}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})$ of bounded constructible complexes on $\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)}$ and its full subcategory

$$ D^{b}_{\{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)\}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\subset D^{b}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)}) $$

of bounded complexes constructible with respect to the $\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)$ -orbits stratification. As a corollary of derived Satake for $U(p,q)$ , we obtain the following constructible description coherent sheaves on $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}^{\prime}$ :

#### Theorem 1.5.1.

(see Theorem 4.3.1) There is an equivalence of dg-categories

$$ D^{b}_{\{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)\}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}^{\prime}) $$

### 1.6. Hermitian symmetric spaces

The symmetric space $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ considered in this paper is a particular example of a Hermitian symmetric space. In forthcoming work [CDMN], we expect to establish Relative Langlands duality for Hermitian symmetric spaces with no roots of type $N$ . Modulo central factors, the Hermitian symmetric spaces under consideration are as follows:

| $X=G/K$ | Rank |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{GL}_{2r+m}/(\mathrm{GL}_{r}\times\mathrm{GL}_{r+m})$ | $r$ |
| $\mathrm{PSO}_{2n}/\mathrm{GSO}_{2n-2}$ | $2$ |
| $\mathrm{SO}_{4r}/\mathrm{GL}_{2r}$ | $r$ |
| $\mathrm{SO}_{4r+2}/\mathrm{GL}_{2r+1}$ | $r$ |
| $E_{6}/\mathrm{GSO}_{10}$ | $2$ |
| $E_{7}/GE_{6}$ | $3$ |

A striking feature of the Hermitian symmetric case is that, after forgetting the gradings, all of the corresponding dual varieties $\check{M}$ are of the form

$$ {\check{G}}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}(V)}(T^{\ast}(V)\times\wedge^{2}(V)\times\mathbf{A}^{a_{X}}) $$

where $V$ is a vector space of dimension $2r$ and $a_{X}$ is the dimension of the remaining affine factor. For the linear periods considered here, $r=p$ and $a_{X}=q-p$ .

## 2. Constructible side

Throughout, sheaves have complex coefficients, and $\mathrm{Rep}(H)$ denotes finite-dimensional algebraic representations of a complex algebraic group $H$ . We use $D^{b}$ for the bounded, finite-rank constructible category and $\mathrm{Perv}$ for its perverse heart. The cocomplete categories $D$ and their compact objects are distinguished below in Section 2.3.

### 2.1. Real groups and symmetric spaces

Let $G=GL_{N}$ be the complex general linear group of rank $N$ . Let $T$ be the diagonal maximal torus and $B=TU$ be the Borel subgroup of upper triangular matrices.

Fix integers $1\leq p\leq q$ and put $N=p+q$ . Consider the following matrix

$$ I_{p,q}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&J_{p}\\
0&I_{q-p}&0\\
J_{p}&0&0\end{pmatrix} $$

where $I_{q-p}$ is the identity matrix of size $q-p$ and $J_{p}$ is the permutation matrix with $1$ ’s on the anti diagonal and $0$ ’s elsewhere. Consider the involution $\theta:G\to G$ given by $\theta(g)=I_{p,q}g(I_{p,q})^{-1}$ . The fixed point subgroup $K=G^{\theta}$ is a Levi symmetric subgroup of $G$ isomorphic to $K\cong GL_{p}\times GL_{q}$ . We denote by $X=G/K$ the associated symmetric space.

The block upper triangular subgroup

$$ P=\begin{pmatrix}B_{p}^{\mathrm{}}&*&*\\
0&GL_{q-p}&*\\
0&0&B_{p}^{\mathrm{}}\end{pmatrix} $$

is a $\theta$ -split minimal parabolic subgroup, where $B_{p}^{\mathrm{}}\subset GL_{p}$ is the upper triangular Borel. Its Levi subgroup is

$$ L=P\cap\theta(P)=\begin{pmatrix}GL_{1}^{p}&0&0\\
0&GL_{q-p}&0\\
0&0&GL_{1}^{p}\end{pmatrix}. $$

The subtorus $A=\{t\in T|\theta(t)=t^{-1}\}^{\circ}\subset T$ is a maximal $\theta$ -split torus consisting of diagonal matrices of the form

$$ \text{diag}(a_{1},...,a_{p},1,...,1,a_{p}^{-1},...,a_{1}^{-1}) $$

We have $L=Z_{G}(A)$ and $P=LU_{P}=MAU_{P}$ where $U_{P}$ is the unipotent radical of $P$ and $M=Z_{K}(A)$ . We see that $X$ is quasi-split (but non-split) if and only if $p=q$ or $p+1=q$ .

We write $\Lambda_{T}=X_{*}(T)$ for the coweight lattice and $\Lambda_{T}^{+}$ for the dominant coweights with respect to $(T,B)$ . Let $2\rho\in X^{*}(T)$ be the sum of the positive roots. The real coweight lattice is $\Lambda_{A}=X_{*}(A)$ , with $\Lambda_{A}^{+}=\Lambda_{A}\cap\Lambda_{T}^{+}$ . Under the coordinate identifications $X_{*}(T)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{N}$ and $X^{*}(T)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{N}$ , we have

$$ 2\rho=(N-1,N-3,\ldots,-N+3,-N+1). $$

The elements of $\Lambda_{A}$ are the tuples

$$ (\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{p},0,\ldots,0,-\lambda_{p},\ldots,-\lambda_{1}). $$

We have an embedding $\tau:X\to G$ sending $x=gK$ to $g\theta(g)^{-1}$ which induces an isomorphism $\tau:X\cong Q=\{g\in G|\theta(g)=g^{-1}\}^{\circ}$ between $X$ and the neutral component of the $\theta$ anti-fixed points in $G$ . We denote by $\iota_{A}:A\to Q\cong X$ the natural embedding.

Consider the conjugation $\eta_{c}:G\to G$ given by $\eta_{c}(g)=(\bar{g}^{t})^{-1}$ with fixed points subgroup $G_{c}=G^{\eta_{c}}=U(N)$ the compact unitary group. Consider the conjugation $\eta:G\to G$ given by $\eta(g)=I_{p,q}(\bar{g}^{-1})^{t}I_{p,q}^{-1}$ . The fixed point subgroup $G^{\eta}$ is a real form of $G$ , denote by $G_{\mathbf{R}}=U(p,q)$ , known as the unitary group of signature $(p,q)$ . Consider the intersections $P_{\mathbf{R}}=P\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ , $L_{\mathbf{R}}=L\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ , and $U_{P,\mathbf{R}}=U_{P}\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ , etc. The intersection $P_{\mathbf{R}}=P\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ is the minimal parabolic subgroup with Iwasawa decomposition $P_{\mathbf{R}}=M_{\mathbf{R}}A_{\mathbf{R}}U_{P,\mathbf{R}}$ . The intersection $K_{c}=K\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ is a maximal compact subgroup isomorphic to the product $K_{c}\cong U(p)\times U(q)$ of unitary groups.

### 2.2. Loop spaces and affine Grassmannians

Let $\mathfrak{L}G$ and $\mathfrak{L}K$ denote the loop groups of $G$ and $K$ , respectively. We also have the arc subgroups $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G\subseteq\mathfrak{L}G$ and $\mathfrak{L}^{+}K\subseteq\mathfrak{L}K$ . Let $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}=\mathfrak{L}G/\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ and $\mathrm{Gr}_{K}=\mathfrak{L}K/\mathfrak{L}^{+}K$ be the corresponding affine Grassmannians. We abbreviate $\mathrm{Gr}=\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . There is a natural closed immersion $\iota_{K}:\mathrm{Gr}_{K}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . Let $\mathfrak{L}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ be the real loop group and $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}\subseteq\mathfrak{L}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ its arc subgroup. The quotient $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}=\mathfrak{L}G_{\mathbf{R}}/\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ is the real affine Grassmannian, a real form of the ind-scheme $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . For any $\lambda\in\Lambda_{T}^{+}$ (resp. $\lambda\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}$ ) we denote by $\mathrm{Gr}^{\lambda}\subset\mathrm{Gr}$ (resp. $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda}\subset\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}$ ) the $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -orbit (resp. $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ ) through $t^{\lambda}$ . We have $\mathrm{Gr}=\bigsqcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}_{T}}\mathrm{Gr}^{\lambda}$ and $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}=\bigsqcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}_{A}}\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda}$ .

Let $\mathfrak{L}X$ be the loop space of $X$ . The embedding $\iota_{A}:A\to X$ of the $\theta$ -split torus gives rise to an embedding $\Lambda_{A}\to\mathfrak{L}X$ sending $\lambda$ to $x^{\lambda}=\iota_{A}(t^{\lambda})$ . Let $\mathfrak{L}X^{\lambda}=\mathfrak{L}^{+}G\cdot x^{\lambda}$ be the $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -orbit through $x^{\lambda}$ . It is known that $\mathfrak{L}X=\bigsqcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}}\mathfrak{L}X^{\lambda}$ and $\overline{\mathfrak{L}X^{\lambda}}=\bigsqcup_{\mu\in\Lambda_{A}^{+},\mu\leq\lambda}\mathfrak{L}X^{\mu}$ (see, e.g., [CY, Proposition 17 and Theorem 18]).

### 2.3. Real and relative Satake categories

Let $(D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}),*)$ be the co-complete monoidal dg category of $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -equivariant constructible complexes on $\mathrm{Gr}$ with monoidal structure given by the convolution product: $F,F^{\prime}\in D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ and $F\star F^{\prime}=m_{!}(F\tilde{\boxtimes}F^{\prime})$ , where $m:\mathfrak{L}G\times^{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}\mathrm{Gr}\to\mathrm{Gr}$ is the natural action map and $F\tilde{\boxtimes}F^{\prime}\in D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}G\times^{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}\mathrm{Gr})$ is the twisted product of $F$ and $F^{\prime}$ . It is known that $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ is compactly generated and we denote by $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})^{c}$ the subcategory of compact objects. The equivariant derived category $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ coincides with the subcategories of locally compact objects11 1 An object $F$ is called locally compact if its image under the forgetful functor $\mathrm{For}:D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})\to D(\mathrm{Gr})$ is compact. and we denote by $\text{Ind}(D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}))$ the ind-completion of $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ . We denote by $(D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}),*),$ etc, the corresponding monoidal categories for $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . We will call the categories $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ , etc (resp. $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})$ , etc) the complex Satake categories for $G$ (resp. real Satake categories for $G_{\mathbf{R}}$ ).

Let $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ be the co-complete dg category of $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -equivariant constructible complexes on $\mathfrak{L}X$ . Denote by $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)^{c}$ , $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}^{b}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ , and $\mathrm{Ind}(D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X))$ for the corresponding categories of compact objects, locally compact objects, and the ind-completion of the latter, respectively. We have a natural action of the complex Satake category

$$ *:D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})\times D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\to D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X) $$

given by $F\star F^{\prime}=a_{!}(F\widetilde{\boxtimes}F^{\prime})$ where $a:\mathfrak{L}G\times^{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}\mathfrak{L}X\to\mathfrak{L}X$ is the action map and $F\widetilde{\boxtimes}F^{\prime}\in D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}G\times^{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}\mathfrak{L}X)$ is the twisted product of $F$ and $F^{\prime}$ . We will call the above category $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ , etc, the relative Satake categories.

### 2.4. Hecke actions

Let $\mathrm{Gr}^{(2)}\to\mathbf{C}$ be the Beilinson-Drinfeld Grassmannian over the complex line classifying triples $(x,E,\phi)$ where $x\in\mathbf{C}$ , $E$ is a $G$ -bundle on $\mathbf{C}$ , and $\phi$ is a trivialization of $E$ on $\mathbf{C}\setminus\{\pm x\}$ . Consider the anti-holomorphic involution $\eta$ on $\mathrm{Gr}^{(2)}$ given by $\eta(x,E,\phi)=(-\bar{x},\eta^{*}E,\eta^{*}\phi)$ defines a real from $\mathrm{Gr}^{(2)}_{\mathbf{R}}\to i\mathbf{R}$ such that

## 3. Spectral side

### 3.1. Hamiltonian dual varieties

We recall the construction in [BZSV] of the Hamiltonian dual variety of $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ . Put $N=p+q$ , $\delta=q-p$ , and $\check{G}=GL_{N}$ . Throughout the spectral calculations, choose the lower triangular Borel $\check{B}$ , with diagonal torus $\check{T}$ and unipotent radical $\check{U}$ , with simple root vectors $E_{i+1,i}$ . For a block of size $m$ , set

$$ \tau_{m}(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t^{1-m},t^{3-m},\ldots,t^{m-1}),\qquad e_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}i(m-i)E_{i+1,i},\qquad f_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}E_{i,i+1}. $$

Thus $(e_{m},[e_{m},f_{m}],f_{m})$ is a principal $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ -triple and $\tau_{m}$ is the sum of the positive coroots for the lower triangular Borel.

Let $\check{L}=I_{2p}\times GL_{\delta}\subset\check{G}$ be the Levi subgroup, and write

$$ \lambda(t)=2\rho_{\check{L}}(t)=\operatorname{diag}(I_{2p},\tau_{\delta}(t)). $$

For $\delta=0$ , put $\lambda=1$ . Choose the principal homomorphism $\iota_{\check{L}}:SL_{2}\to\check{L}$ whose differentials on the upper and lower root vectors are $e_{\delta}$ and $f_{\delta}$ , respectively, and whose restriction to the diagonal torus is $\lambda$ . For $\delta\leq 1$ this homomorphism is trivial. Let $\check{P}_{X}=\check{L}_{X}\check{N}_{X}$ be the parabolic determined by $\lambda$ : its Lie algebra is the sum of the nonnegative weight spaces, $\check{L}_{X}=Z_{\check{G}}(\lambda)$ , and $\operatorname{Lie}\check{N}_{X}$ is the sum of the positive weight spaces. Explicitly,

$$ \check{L}_{X}\cong\begin{cases}GL_{2p}\times GL_{1}^{q-p},&p+q\in 2\mathbb{Z},\\
GL_{2p+1}\times GL_{1}^{q-p-1},&p+q\in 2\mathbb{Z}+1.\end{cases} $$

We will use the distinguished commuting subgroup

$$ \check{L}^{\prime}_{X}=GL_{2p}\times I_{q-p}\cong GL_{2p}. $$

Let $V=\mathbb{C}^{2p}$ , with standard basis $\mathbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{e}_{2p}$ and the symplectic form characterized by $\omega(\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{e}_{2p+1-i})=1$ for $1\leq i\leq p$ , skew-symmetry, and zero on all other pairs of basis vectors. The dual group of $X$ is

$$ \check{G}_{X}=\mathrm{Sp}(V)\subset\check{L}^{\prime}_{X}\subset\check{G}. $$

The block $GL_{2p}$ commutes with $\iota_{\check{L}}(SL_{2})$ , so

$$ \rho_{X}:\check{G}_{X}\times SL_{2}\longrightarrow\check{G},\qquad(g,h)\longmapsto g\,\iota_{\check{L}}(h) $$

is the Arthur homomorphism associated to $X$ .

Denote by $\check{\mathfrak{g}},\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X},\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}$ , etc, the Lie algebra of $\check{G}$ , $\check{G}_{X}$ , $\check{N}_{X}$ , etc. Let $\Phi_{\mathrm{tr}}:\check{\mathfrak{g}}\cong\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ be the $\check{G}$ -equivariant isomorphism induced by the trace paring. Let $e_{X}=d\iota_{\check{L}}(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix})$ and $y_{X}=d\iota_{\check{L}}(\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix})$ , and $\psi_{X}=\Phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(y_{X})\in\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ . Denote by $\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}\subset\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}$ be the $\geq 2$ weight subspace with respect to the action of $\lambda$ . Put $\check{N}_{X,\geq 2}=\exp(\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2})$ . Following [BZSV, Section 3.4.2], we will consider the following three Hamiltonian varieties:

- (1) the cotangent bundle $T^{*}\check{G}$ viewed as $\check{G}\times\check{G}$ -Hamiltonian space with moment map $T^{*}\check{G}\cong\check{G}\times\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}\times\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ sending $(g,v)\to(\text{Ad}_{g}v,-v)$ (here we identify $\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ as left invariant differential forms on $\check{G}$ ).

- (2) the symplectic representation $\check{S}_{X}$ of $\check{G}_{X}=\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}$ given by

$$ \check{S}_{X}=\begin{cases}T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}\ \ \ \ p=q,\\ 0\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ p\neq q.\end{cases} $$

where $T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}$ is the cotangent bundle of the standard representation $\mathbb{A}^{2p}$ of $\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}$ , viewed as $\check{G}_{X}$ -Hamiltonian space with the standard moment map $\check{S}_{X}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}^{*}=\mathfrak{sp}_{2p}^{*}$ sending $s\in\check{S}_{X}$ to $(v\to\frac{1}{2}\omega_{\check{S}_{X}}(vs,s))\in\mathfrak{sp}_{2p}^{*}$ (here $\omega_{\check{S}_{X}}$ is the canonical symplectic form on $T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}$ )

- (3) the quotient space $\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}$ with the symplectic form $\omega_{\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}}(u,u^{\prime})=\psi_{X}([u,u^{\prime}])$ and the Hamiltonian $\check{G}_{X}\check{N}_{X}$ -action given by (i) the $\check{G}_{X}$ -action is through the adjoint action (ii) the $\check{N}_{X}$ -action is through the translation action $\check{N}_{X}/\check{N}_{X,\geq 2}\cong\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}$ (iii) the $\check{G}_{X}$ -moment map is given by

$$ \check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}\to\mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{Sp}(\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}))^{*}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}_{X} $$

where the first map the canonical moment map on the symplectic vector space and the second map is induced by the inclusion $\check{G}_{X}\to\mathrm{Sp}(\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}))$ (iv) the $\check{N}_{X}$ -moment map is given by $\psi_{X}$ -shifted moment map

$$ \check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}\cong(\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2})^{*}\to\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}^{*}\ \ \ v\to v+\psi_{X}|_{\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}} $$

where the first isomorphism is induced by the symplectic form.

#### Example 3.1.1.

(1) Assume $p+q$ is odd. Then we have $\check{S}_{X}=0$ . Moreover, it follows from (8) that the weights with respect to co-character $2\rho_{\check{L}}$ are all even numbers and it follows that $\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}=0$

(2) Assume $p+q$ is even. If $p=q$ , then we have $\check{S}_{X}\cong T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}$ and $\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}=0$ . If $p\neq q$ , then we have $\check{S}_{X}=0$ and a direct computation show that $\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}$ -equivariant isomorphism

$$ \check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}\cong\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,1}\cong T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}. $$

where $\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,1}$ is the weight one subspace.

The product space

$$ T^{*}\check{G}\times\check{S}_{X}\times\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2} $$

is naturally a Hamiltonain $\check{G}_{X}\check{N}_{X}$ -space, where $\check{N}_{X}$ acts trivially on $\check{S}_{X}$ and $\check{G}_{X}\check{N}_{X}\subset\check{G}$ acts on $T^{*}\check{G}$ through the right $\check{G}$ -action, with moment map

$$ \mu_{\psi_{X}}:T^{*}\check{G}\times\check{S}_{X}\times\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}^{*}\times\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}^{*} $$

and the dual variety of $X$ is defined as the following Hamiltonian reduction

$$ \check{M}=\mu^{-1}_{\psi_{X}}(0)\sslash\check{G}_{X}\check{N}_{X}=T^{*}\check{G}\times_{\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}^{*}\times\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}^{*}}^{\check{G}_{X}\check{N}_{X}}(\check{S}_{X}\times\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}) $$

We have the residual moment map

$$ \mu:\check{M}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*} $$

coming from the left $\check{G}$ -action on $T^{*}\check{G}$ . Moreover, $\mu$ is $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -equivariant with respect to the square action on $\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ and the $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ on $\check{M}$ induced by

- (1) the scalar action on $\check{S}_{X}$ and $\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X}/\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X,\geq 2}$

- (2) the action on $T^{*}\check{G}\cong\check{G}\times\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ given by $t(g,v)=(g2\rho_{\check{L}}(t^{-1}),t^{2}\text{Ad}_{2\rho_{\check{L}}(t)}(v)).$

#### Example 3.1.2.

(1) Assume $p+q$ is odd. Then it follows from Example (3.1.1) that

$$ \check{M}\cong T^{*}_{\psi_{X}}(GL_{p+q}/\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}\check{N}_{X})\cong GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}\check{N}_{X}}(\psi_{X}+(\mathfrak{sp}_{2p}\oplus\check{\mathfrak{n}}_{X})^{\perp}) $$

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{2p}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}X&Y\\

Here $r(X)=J_{p}X^{t}J_{p}$ is reflection across the anti-diagonal, with $J_{p}$ the anti-diagonal permutation matrix. The invariant ring for the diagonal action of $\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}$ on $\mathfrak{p}_{2p}\times V\times V$ is polynomial, with generators $b_{1},\ldots,b_{p},c_{0},\ldots,c_{p-1}$ characterized by

$$ \det(z-T)=P(z)^{2},\quad P(z)=z^{p}+b_{1}z^{p-1}+\cdots+b_{p},\qquad c_{j}=-\omega(T^{j}u,v). $$

Here $(T,u,v)\in\mathfrak{p}_{2p}\times V\times V$ . The quotient map is equidimensional; see [S] and [Kn2].

Recall that $\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{m}}=\mathfrak{gl}_{m}\sslash GL_{m}$ is the coefficient space of monic polynomials of degree $m$ , with origin $z^{m}$ . Using the trace identification, let $\chi_{m}:\mathfrak{gl}_{m}^{*}\to\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{m}}$ be the characteristic-polynomial quotient map. We use the coordinates $c_{0},\ldots,c_{p-1}$ for a second copy of $\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}$ by associating to them the polynomial

$$ C(z)=z^{p}+c_{0}z^{p-1}+\cdots+c_{p-1}. $$

The final factor $\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{\delta}}$ has coordinates $d_{1},\ldots,d_{\delta}$ , with

$$ D(z)=z^{\delta}+d_{1}z^{\delta-1}+\cdots+d_{\delta}; $$

for $\delta=0$ this factor is a point and $D=1$ . Lemma 3.2.1 and Proposition 3.2.2 give the natural product presentations

$$ \displaystyle(\mathfrak{p}_{2p}\times V\times V)\sslash\mathrm{Sp}_{2p} \displaystyle\simeq\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}},\ \ \ \check{M}\sslash\check{G} \displaystyle\simeq\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{\delta}}. $$

In particular,

$$ \mathcal{O}(\check{M})^{\check{G}}=\mathbb{C}[b_{1},\ldots,b_{p},c_{0},\ldots,c_{p-1},d_{1},\ldots,d_{\delta}]. $$

The grading transported from $\check{M}$ is

$$ \deg b_{i}=2i,\qquad\deg c_{j}=2(j+\delta+1),\qquad\deg d_{i}=2i. $$

Denote these quotient maps by

$$ \chi_{p,p}:\mathfrak{p}_{2p}\times V\times V\to\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}},\ \ \ \ \chi_{\check{M}}:\check{M}\to\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{\delta}}. $$

We next construct sections of $\chi_{p,p}$ and $\chi_{\check{M}}$ using the companion-matrix description. For $b=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{p})$ , take the companion matrix

$$ \kappa_{p}(b)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\cdots&0&-b_{p}\\
1&0&\cdots&0&-b_{p-1}\\
0&1&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0&-b_{2}\\
0&\cdots&0&1&-b_{1}\end{pmatrix}. $$

#### Lemma 3.3.1.

- (1) The map

$$ \kappa_{p,p}(b,c)=\left(\begin{pmatrix}\kappa_{p}(b)&0\\ 0&r(\kappa_{p}(b))\end{pmatrix},\,\mathbf{e}_{1},\,(0,\ldots,0,-c_{p-1},\ldots,-c_{0})^{t}\right) $$

is an algebraic section of $\chi_{p,p}$ .

- (2) In the product fiber coordinates above, the map $\kappa_{\check{M}}=\kappa_{p,p}\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{\delta}}}$ , $\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{\delta}}$ $\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\ \kappa_{\check{M}}\ }\check{V}_{X}$ $\displaystyle\hookrightarrow GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}\check{V}_{X}\simeq\check{M},$ defines an algebraic section of $\chi_{\check{M}}$ , with the final factor omitted when $\delta=0$ .

Write $\kappa_{p,p}(b,c)=(T,u,v)$ . The characteristic polynomial of $T$ is $(z^{p}+b_{1}z^{p-1}+\cdots+b_{p})^{2}$ . Since $T^{j}u=\mathbf{e}_{j+1}$ for $0\leq j<p$ , we also have $-\omega(T^{j}u,v)=c_{j}$ . This proves (1); part (2) follows immediately from part (1). ∎

The moment map $\mu:\check{M}\to\mathfrak{gl}_{p+q}^{*}$ is $GL_{p+q}$ -equivariant and hence gives rise to the following commutative diagram:

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\check{M}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{gl}_{p+q}^{*}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p}}\times\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{\delta}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{c}_{GL_{p+q}}.} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mu} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi_{\check{M}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi_{N}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bar{\mu}} $$

Let $\mathcal{N}_{\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}}=\chi_{N}^{-1}(0)$ be the nilpotent cone for $\mathfrak{gl}_{p+q}^{*}$ , and put $\mathcal{N}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}=\chi_{p,p}^{-1}(0)$ , the exotic null-cone in this representation; see [Ka]. It follows from Proposition 3.2.2 that

$$ \chi_{\check{M}}^{-1}(0)\simeq GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}\mathcal{N}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}. $$

Consider the preimage $\mu^{-1}(\mathcal{N}_{\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}})\subset\check{M}$ of the nilpotent cone under the moment map.

#### Lemma 3.3.2.

The natural closed embedding

$$ GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}\mathcal{N}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}\simeq\chi_{\check{M}}^{-1}(0)\hookrightarrow\mu^{-1}(\mathcal{N}_{\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}}) $$

induces a bijection on $\mathbb{C}$ -points.

#### Proof.

Denote by $\bar{\mu}$ the lower arrow in (15). In view of the commutativity of that diagram, it suffices to show that the $\mathbb{C}$ -points of $\bar{\mu}^{-1}(0)$ consist only of the origin. By Lemma 3.3.1, we have

$$ \bar{\mu}(b,c,d)=\chi_{N}\circ\mu\circ\kappa_{\check{M}}(b,c,d), $$

and $\bar{\mu}(b,c,d)=0$ if and only if the characteristic polynomial of $\mu(\kappa_{\check{M}}(b,c,d))$ is $z^{p+q}$ . Thus we reduce to checking that

$$ \det\bigl(z-\mu(\kappa_{\check{M}}(b,c,d))\bigr)=z^{p+q}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(b,c,d)=0. $$

Write $\kappa_{\check{M}}(b,c,d)=(T,u,v,d)$ , put $K_{b}=\kappa_{p}(b)$ , and set

$$ R(c)=\begin{pmatrix}c_{0}&\cdots&c_{p-1}\\
0&\cdots&0\\
\vdots&&\vdots\\
0&\cdots&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

Then equations (9) and (14) imply

$$ \mu(\kappa_{\check{M}}(b,c,d))=\begin{cases}\begin{pmatrix}K_{b}+R(c)&0\\
0&r(K_{b})\end{pmatrix},&p=q,\\[8.0pt]
\begin{pmatrix}K_{b}&0&E_{p,\delta}\\
0&r(K_{b})&0\\
F_{\delta,p}(c)&0&f_{\delta}+s(d)\end{pmatrix},&p<q.\end{cases} $$

Here $E_{p,\delta}$ is $p\times\delta$ with its only nonzero entry $1$ in position $(1,1)$ , and $F_{\delta,p}(c)$ is $\delta\times p$ with last row $(c_{0},\ldots,c_{p-1})$ and all other rows zero. For $\delta>0$ , $s(d)\in Z_{\mathfrak{gl}_{\delta}}(e_{\delta})$ is the unique element such that $\det(z-f_{\delta}-s(d))=D(z)$ .

First, in both cases $r(K_{b})$ is a direct summand of the moment matrix. If the moment matrix is nilpotent, then $r(K_{b})$ is nilpotent. Since

$$ \det(z-r(K_{b}))=z^{p}+b_{1}z^{p-1}+\cdots+b_{p}, $$

this forces $b=0$ .

With $b=0$ , expansion of the displayed determinants gives

$$ \det\bigl(z-\mu(\kappa_{\check{M}}(0,c,d))\bigr)=z^{p}\left(z^{p}D(z)-\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}c_{j}z^{p-1-j}\right),\qquad D=1\text{ if }\delta=0. $$

Thus nilpotency is equivalent to

$$ z^{p}D(z)-\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}c_{j}z^{p-1-j}=z^{q}. $$

The term $z^{p}D(z)$ has no powers of degree below $p$ , so comparison of those coefficients gives $c=0$ . We then obtain $D(z)=z^{q-p}=z^{\delta}$ , hence $d=0$ . Conversely, the same formula gives $z^{p+q}$ when $(b,c,d)=0$ . This proves the lemma. ∎

### 3.4. Whittaker cotangent bundles

Let $\check{K}=GL_{p}\times GL_{q}$ and let $\check{P}$ be the lower triangular parabolic with Levi $\check{K}$ . Put

$$ f_{p,q}=\operatorname{diag}(f_{p},f_{q}),\qquad\tau_{\check{K}}(t)=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_{p}(t),\tau_{q}(t)),\qquad\tau_{\check{G}}(t)=\tau_{N}(t). $$

The additive character $\psi_{\check{K}}:\check{U}\to\mathbb{G}_{a}$ has differential $u\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(f_{p,q}u)$ : it is $1$ on the pinned simple root vectors in $\check{K}$ and $0$ on the simple root vectors outside $\check{K}$ . For the right action $g\mapsto gu^{-1}$ , the Whittaker cotangent bundle is the Hamiltonian reduction at $-d\psi_{\check{K}}$ :

$$ T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})\simeq\check{G}\times^{\check{U}}(f_{p,q}+\check{\mathfrak{b}}) $$

with moment map sending $[g,x]$ to $\operatorname{Ad}_{g}x$ . The grading relevant to the dual variety is defined by

$$ \gamma(t)=\tau_{\check{K}}(t)^{2}\tau_{\check{G}}(t)^{-1}=\tau_{\check{K}}(t)\operatorname{diag}(t^{q}I_{p},t^{-p}I_{q}), $$

and

$$ t[g,x]=[g\gamma(t)^{-1},t^{2}\operatorname{Ad}_{\gamma(t)}x]. $$

### 3.5. Regular centralizers

We recall some facts and constructions related to the group scheme of regular centralizers (see, e.g., [BF, Kn1, Ngo, Gi, L]). Let $J_{\check{G}}\to\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}}$ (resp. $J_{\check{K}}\to\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}$ ) be the group scheme of regular centralizers of $\check{G}$ (resp. $\check{K}$ ). Choose the homogeneous Kostant sections $\kappa_{\check{G}}:\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ and $\kappa_{\check{K}}:\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}\to\check{\mathfrak{k}}^{*}$ , whose images on a block of size $m$ are $f_{m}+Z_{\mathfrak{gl}_{m}}(e_{m})$ . They give rise to closed embeddings

$$ J_{\check{G}}\longrightarrow\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}}\times\check{G},\qquad J_{\check{K}}\longrightarrow\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}\times\check{K}. $$

The fiber over $x$ is the centralizer of $\kappa_{\check{G}}(x)$ , respectively of $\kappa_{\check{K}}(x)$ . Moreover, we have natural isomorphisms

$$ \operatorname{Lie}J_{\check{G}}\simeq T^{*}\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}},\qquad\operatorname{Lie}J_{\check{K}}\simeq T^{*}\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}. $$

For $A=\check{G},\check{K}$ , the chosen sections satisfy

$$ \kappa_{A}(t^{2}x)=t^{2}\operatorname{Ad}_{\tau_{A}(t)}\kappa_{A}(x), $$

where $t^{2}x$ denotes square dilation on the Chevalley quotient.

The embedding $\check{K}\to\check{G}$ gives rise to the map between Chevalley quotients

$$ \pi:\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}=\check{\mathfrak{k}}^{*}\sslash\check{K}\longrightarrow\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}\sslash\check{G}=\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}}, $$

and hence to the cotangent map

$$ \pi^{*}\operatorname{Lie}J_{\check{G}}\simeq\pi^{*}T^{*}\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}}\longrightarrow T^{*}\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}\simeq\operatorname{Lie}J_{\check{K}}. $$

As in [L] and [Gi, Proposition 5.4.1], this map is the differential of a homomorphism

$$ \alpha:\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}\longrightarrow J_{\check{K}} $$

of group schemes over $\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}$ . Note that $\pi$ is generically étale and the map (18) is generically an isomorphism.

Using the above homomorphism, we can form the quotient

$$ (\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}=\bigl((\check{G}\times\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}})\times_{\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}}J_{\check{K}}\bigr)/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}} $$

by the group scheme $\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}$ over $\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}$ . Its action on the two factors is through the Kostant-section embedding and the homomorphism (18), respectively; explicitly,

$$ (g,x,y)\cdot j=(gj^{-1},x,\alpha(j)y). $$

We have a natural $\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -action on this quotient, given by

$$ (h,t)[g,x,y]=[hg\tau_{\check{G}}(t)^{-1},t^{2}x,\operatorname{Ad}_{\tau_{\check{K}}(t)}y], $$

and a $\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -equivariant map

$$ (\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}\longrightarrow\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*},\qquad[g,x,y]\longmapsto\operatorname{Ad}_{g}\kappa_{\check{G}}(\pi(x)). $$

The morphism (19) extends to a $\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -equivariant map $\overline{(\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ .

#### Proposition 3.5.1.

There is a $\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -equivariant isomorphism of affine varieties over $\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$

$$ \overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})}\simeq\overline{(\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}, $$

with the grading (17) on the left.

#### Proof.

According to [Ga, Theorem 1.1], there is a $\check{G}\times\check{K}$ -equivariant isomorphism over $\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$

$$ \overline{T^{*}(\check{G}/\check{U}_{\check{P}})}\simeq\overline{(\check{G}\times\check{K}\times\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}, $$

where $\check{U}_{\check{P}}\subset\check{P}$ is the unipotent radical. Taking Whittaker reduction with respect to $\check{K}$ and $\psi_{\check{K}}$ , we obtain the desired isomorphism

$$ \displaystyle\overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})} \displaystyle\simeq\overline{T^{*}(\check{G}/\check{U}_{\check{P}})\sslash_{-d\psi_{\check{K}}}\check{U}_{\check{K}}} \displaystyle\simeq\overline{(\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}. $$

Here $\check{U}_{\check{K}}=\check{U}\cap\check{K}$ , the differential is restricted to $\operatorname{Lie}\check{U}_{\check{K}}$ , and the sign is that of the right action $g\mapsto gh^{-1}$ . The first isomorphism follows from [M, Lemma 3.1.10]; the second is the Whittaker reduction of Gannon’s theorem, as in [Ga, Corollary 2.8]. ∎

There is a $\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -equivariant isomorphism of affine varieties over $\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$

### 3.7. Generalized Kostant theorem

For $m\geq 1$ , let $\check{B}_{m}\subseteq GL_{m}$ be the lower triangular Borel, let $\check{U}_{m}$ be its unipotent radical, and write $\check{\mathfrak{b}}_{m}$ and $\check{\mathfrak{u}}_{m}$ for their Lie algebras. Consider the regular nilpotent matrices

$$ e_{m}=\begin{pmatrix}0&&&&\\
m-1&0&&&\\
&2(m-2)&0&&\\
&&\ddots&\ddots&\\
&&&m-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad f_{m}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&&&\\
&0&1&&\\
&&\ddots&\ddots&\\
&&&0&1\\
&&&&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

Put

$$ \tau_{m}(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t^{1-m},t^{3-m},\ldots,t^{m-1}). $$

Thus $(e_{m},d\tau_{m}(1),f_{m})$ is a principal $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ -triple. The celebrated result of Kostant [K] asserts that $\check{U}_{m}$ acts freely on $\check{\mathfrak{b}}_{m}+f_{m}$ and provides a transverse slice to the $\check{U}_{m}$ -orbits. More precisely, let $\mathcal{S}_{m}=Z_{\mathfrak{gl}_{m}}(e_{m})\subseteq\check{\mathfrak{b}}_{m}$ . Then the action map

$$ \check{U}_{m}\times(\mathcal{S}_{m}+f_{m})\longrightarrow\check{\mathfrak{b}}_{m}+f_{m},\qquad(u,x)\longmapsto\operatorname{Ad}_{u}(x), $$

is a $U_{m}$ -equivariant isomorphism.

The main result of this section is an analog of Kostant’s theorem in which $f_{m}$ is replaced by a nilpotent element with two Jordan blocks. Namely, consider the following nilpotent elements

$$ e_{p,q}=\begin{pmatrix}e_{p}&0\\
0&e_{q}\end{pmatrix},\qquad f_{p,q}=\begin{pmatrix}f_{p}&0\\
0&f_{q}\end{pmatrix}. $$

The second matrix is the trace representative of $d\psi_{\check{K}}$ used in Section 3.4. We have a natural adjoint action of $\check{U}$ on $\check{\mathfrak{b}}+f_{p,q}$ but, unlike the setting of Kostant theorem, this action is typically not free. We shall introduce a subgroup $\check{U}_{X}\subseteq\check{U}$ and a $\check{U}_{X}$ -invariant affine subspace $\mathcal{S}_{p,q}+f_{p,q}\subseteq\check{\mathfrak{b}}+f_{p,q}$ . The generalized Kostant theorem, see Theorem 3.7.5 below, says that the adjoint action map factors through an isomorphism

$$ \check{U}\times^{\check{U}_{X}}(\mathcal{S}_{p,q}+f_{p,q})\simeq\check{\mathfrak{b}}+f_{p,q}. $$

#### 3.7.1. Symplectic linear algebra

We record some linear algebra results needed for the proof of (20). We focus on the case $p=q$ and write $\check{G}=GL_{2p}(\mathbf{C})$ . Let $V=\mathbf{C}^{2p}$ , and let $\mathbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{e}_{2p}$ be its standard basis. Equip $V$ with the symplectic form $\omega(\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{e}_{2p+1-i})=1$ for $1\leq i\leq p$ , the remaining pairings being determined by alternatingness and zero. Write

$$ \Omega=\begin{pmatrix}0&J_{p}\\
-J_{p}&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\check{G}_{X}=\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}=\check{G}^{\theta_{X}},\qquad\theta_{X}(g)=\Omega^{-1}(g^{\mathrm{t}})^{-1}\Omega, $$

where $J_{p}$ is the reversing matrix of size $p$ . The induced involution on $\check{\mathfrak{g}}$ gives $\check{\mathfrak{g}}=\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}\oplus\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ , with $\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}=\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{\theta_{X}}$ and $\mathfrak{p}_{2p}=\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{-\theta_{X}}$ . If $r(A)=J_{p}A^{\mathrm{t}}J_{p}$ , then

$$ \theta_{X}\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\
C&D\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-r(D)&r(B)\\
r(C)&-r(A)\end{pmatrix}. $$

Let $\check{B}$ be the lower triangular Borel, $\check{U}$ its unipotent radical, and $\check{T}$ the diagonal torus. These subgroups are $\theta_{X}$ -stable. Put $\check{U}_{X}=\check{U}\cap\check{G}_{X}=\check{U}^{\theta_{X}}$ and $\check{\mathfrak{u}}_{X}=\operatorname{Lie}(\check{U}_{X})$ . Let $\check{B}^{-}$ be the opposite Borel and $\check{U}^{-}$ its unipotent radical. Write $V=W_{1}\oplus W_{2}$ for the two coordinate subspaces of dimension $p$ . Let $\check{P}\supseteq\check{B}$ be the parabolic stabilizing $W_{2}$ , let $\check{U}_{\check{P}}$ be its unipotent radical, and let $\check{K}=GL_{p}\times GL_{p}$ be its Levi subgroup preserving $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ .

Using the weighted matrices fixed above, define

$$ e=\begin{pmatrix}e_{p}&0\\
0&e_{p}\end{pmatrix},\qquad f=\begin{pmatrix}f_{p}&0\\
0&f_{p}\end{pmatrix}=f_{p,p},\qquad h=[e,f]. $$

Then $(e,h,f)$ is a principal $\mathfrak{sl}_{2}$ -triple in $\check{\mathfrak{k}}=\operatorname{Lie}(\check{K})$ . The element $h$ is the differential of the cocharacter $\operatorname{diag}(\tau_{p},\tau_{p})$ , which is the sum of the positive coroots of $\check{K}$ . The block formula for $\theta_{X}$ shows that $e,f\in\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ and hence $h\in\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}$ . Consequently, $[f,\check{\mathfrak{u}}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p}]\subseteq\check{\mathfrak{b}}\cap\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}=\check{\mathfrak{b}}^{\theta_{X}}$ .

#### Lemma 3.7.1.

The map $\operatorname{ad}_{f}:\check{\mathfrak{u}}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p}\to\check{\mathfrak{b}}^{\theta_{X}}$ is injective.

#### Proof.

If $x\in\check{\mathfrak{u}}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ satisfies $[f,x]=0$ , then its image under the projection $\pi:\operatorname{Lie}(\check{P})\twoheadrightarrow\check{\mathfrak{k}}$ does the same. But $\pi(x)$ belongs to $\check{\mathfrak{u}}\cap\check{\mathfrak{k}}$ and $f\in\check{\mathfrak{u}}^{-}\cap\check{\mathfrak{k}}$ is a regular nilpotent in $\check{\mathfrak{k}}$ , so $\pi(x)=0$ . Therefore $x\in\operatorname{Lie}(\check{U}_{\check{P}})$ .

We have a $\check{P}$ -equivariant isomorphism $\operatorname{Lie}(\check{U}_{\check{P}})\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(V/W_{2},W_{2})$ and therefore an $\check{K}$ -equivariant isomorphism $\operatorname{Lie}(\check{U}_{\check{P}})\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(W_{1},W_{2})$ . Let $\check{K}_{\Delta}\subseteq\check{K}$ be the diagonal subgroup. Then $W_{1}\simeq W_{2}$ as $\check{K}_{\Delta}$ -modules, and $\operatorname{Lie}(\check{U}_{\check{P}})$ is isomorphic to the adjoint representation of $\check{K}_{\Delta}$ . Observe that $f\in\check{\mathfrak{k}}_{\Delta}$ is principal nilpotent in this reductive subalgebra. Hence its centralizer is spanned by its powers. Thus the kernel of $\operatorname{ad}_{f}$ on $\operatorname{Lie}(\check{U}_{\check{P}})$ consists of matrices

$$ x=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
C&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad f_{p}C=Cf_{p}, $$

where $C\in\mathbf{C}[f_{p}]$ is upper triangular and constant along each diagonal. But then $r(C)=J_{p}C^{\mathrm{t}}J_{p}=C$ , so $x$ is $\theta_{X}$ -invariant. Since $x\in\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ , we conclude that $x=0$ . ∎

Now we will construct a complement to the image $\operatorname{ad}_{f}(\check{\mathfrak{u}}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p})$ in $\check{\mathfrak{b}}^{\theta_{X}}$ . We have the moment map $V\times V^{*}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}^{*}$ . Using the trace form, we identify $\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}$ with $\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}^{*}$ . We also use $w\mapsto\omega(w,-)$ to make the $\check{G}_{X}$ -equivariant identification $V\simeq V^{*}$ . We obtain a $\check{G}_{X}$ -equivariant symmetric bilinear pairing

$$ \beta(v,w)\in\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X},\qquad\beta(v,w)(z)=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\omega(w,z)v+\omega(v,z)w\bigr). $$

We define a map $i:V\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}$ by $i(w)=\beta(\mathbf{e}_{2p},w)$ . Since $\mathbf{e}_{2p}$ is $\check{U}$ -invariant, $i$ is $\check{U}_{X}$ -equivariant. The map $i$ is injective, because $\beta$ identifies $\operatorname{Sym}^{2}V$ with $\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}$ . Let $\mathfrak{v}=i(V)$ be its image. It is a $\check{U}_{X}$ -stable subspace of $\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}$ and consists of the $\theta_{X}$ -fixed matrices supported in the first column and last row. In particular, $\mathfrak{v}\subseteq\check{\mathfrak{b}}^{\theta_{X}}$ .

#### Lemma 3.7.2.

$\mathfrak{v}\cap[f,\check{\mathfrak{u}}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p}]=0$ .

#### Proof.

Write

$$ x=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\
C&r(A)\end{pmatrix}\in\check{\mathfrak{u}}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p}, $$

where $A$ is strictly lower triangular and $r(C)=-C$ . Suppose $[f,x]\in\mathfrak{v}$ . Its upper-left block is supported in the first column, say $[f_{p},A]=d\varepsilon_{1}^{\mathrm{t}}$ , where $\varepsilon_{1}=(1,0,\ldots,0)^{\mathrm{t}}\in\mathbb{C}^{p}$ . For $0\leq k<p$ ,

$$ 0=\operatorname{tr}(f_{p}^{k}[f_{p},A])=\varepsilon_{1}^{\mathrm{t}}f_{p}^{k}d=d_{k+1}. $$

Hence $[f_{p},A]=0$ and $A=0$ . The lower-left block $[f_{p},C]$ is supported in its first column and last row, so $C_{a+1,b}=C_{a,b-1}$ for $a<p$ and $b>1$ . Thus $C$ is constant along each diagonal, which implies $r(C)=C$ . Together with $r(C)=-C$ this gives $C=0$ . ∎

#### Corollary 3.7.3.

$\check{\mathfrak{b}}^{\theta_{X}}=\mathfrak{v}\oplus[f,\check{\mathfrak{u}}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p}]$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 3.7.2, it now suffices to count dimensions. On one hand,

$$ \dim\check{\mathfrak{b}}^{\theta_{X}}=\frac{\dim\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}+\operatorname{rank}\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{X}}{2}=\frac{p(2p+1)+p}{2}=p^{2}+p. $$

Letting $\check{G}_{X,v_{0}}$ denote the stabilizer of $v_{0}$ in $\check{G}_{X}$ , we see that it suffices to show that the action map $\check{G}_{X,v_{0}}\times((\check{\mathfrak{b}}+f)\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p})\to\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ is surjective up to a codimension at least two subvariety. To this end, define $\ell:\mathfrak{p}_{2p}\to\mathbf{Z}$ by setting $\ell(x)$ to be the dimension of the subspace $V_{x}$ spanned by $v:=v_{0},xv,x^{2}v,\ldots$ . It is clear that the fibers of $\ell$ are locally closed subvarieties of $\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ .

#### Lemma 3.8.3.

Let $x\in\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ and $w\in V$ . The subspace spanned by $x^{i}w$ for $i\geq 0$ is isotropic.

#### Proof.

We have $\omega(x^{i}w,x^{j}w)=\omega(w,x^{i+j}w)=\omega(x^{j}w,x^{i}w)$ by the self-adjointness of $x$ . But $\omega(x^{i}w,x^{j}w)=-\omega(x^{j}w,x^{i}w)$ , since $\omega$ is alternating. So $\omega(x^{i}w,x^{j}w)=0$ . ∎

#### Lemma 3.8.4.

The bound $\ell(x)\leq p$ holds for $x\in\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ . Moreover, it is attained over an open dense subvariety of $\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 3.8.3, the subspace $V_{x}$ is isotropic. So $\ell(x)=\dim V_{x}\leq\dim V/2=p$ . Therefore $\ell^{-1}(p)$ is open. It is nonempty because $\ell(f)=p$ . The density follows from the irreducibility of $\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ . ∎

Let $\mathcal{U}:=\ell^{-1}(p)$ be the dense open subvariety of Lemma 3.8.4.

#### Lemma 3.8.5.

Let $V$ be a symplectic vector space of dimension $2p$ and let $0\leq i\leq p$ . Then the variety $Gr_{i}^{\omega}$ of $i$ -dimensional isotropic subspaces $W\subseteq V$ has dimension

$$ \dim Gr_{i}^{\omega}=i\left(2p-\frac{3i-1}{2}\right). $$

#### Proof.

The case $i=0$ is immediate. Let $Fl_{i}^{\omega}$ denote the variety of isotropic flags in $V$ of height $i$ . There is a smooth surjection $Fl_{i}^{\omega}\to Gr_{i}^{\omega}$ whose fiber over $W$ is the variety $Fl(W)$ of complete flags in $W$ . Hence

$$ \dim Gr_{i}^{\omega}=\dim Fl_{i}^{\omega}-\dim Fl(W). $$

Recall that $\dim Fl(W)=i(i-1)/2$ . The natural map $Fl_{i}^{\omega}\to Fl_{i-1}^{\omega}$ has fiber over $W_{\bullet}$ isomorphic to $\mathbf{P}(W_{i-1}^{\perp}/W_{i-1})$ , of dimension $2p-2(i-1)-1$ . So

$$ \dim Fl_{i}^{\omega}=\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}(2p-2j-1)=(2p-i)i. $$

Therefore

$$ \dim Gr_{i}^{\omega}=(2p-i)i-\frac{i(i-1)}{2}=i\left(2p-\frac{3i-1}{2}\right). $$

∎

#### Lemma 3.8.6.

For $1\leq i\leq p$ , we have

$$ \operatorname{codim}_{\mathfrak{p}_{2p}}\ell^{-1}(i)=2(p-i). $$

In particular, $\dim\ell^{-1}(i)\leq\dim\mathfrak{p}_{2p}-2$ for $i<p$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{Y}$ be the variety of isotropic subspaces of $V$ of dimension $i$ containing $v$ . There is a map $\pi:\ell^{-1}(i)\to\mathcal{Y}$ taking $x$ to $V_{x}$ . This map is surjective. Indeed, suppose that $W$ is any such subspace. We may choose a symplectic basis $v_{1},\ldots,v_{2p}=v$ such that $W$ is spanned by $v_{2p},\ldots,v_{2p-i+1}$ . Let $x$ operate on $V$ by $xv_{j}=v_{j-1}$ for $j\geq 2p-i+2$ or $2\leq j\leq i$ , and $xv_{j}=0$ otherwise. Then $x\in\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ , $x\in\ell^{-1}(i)$ , and $\pi(x)=W$ .

Now we compute $\dim\mathcal{Y}$ . Let $L$ be the span of $v$ . Then isotropic $i$ -planes $W$ containing $L$ correspond to isotropic $(i-1)$ -planes $W/L$ in the symplectic vector space $L^{\perp}/L$ , of dimension $2p-2$ . By Lemma 3.8.5,

$$ \dim\mathcal{Y}=(i-1)\left(2p-2-\frac{3(i-1)-1}{2}\right)=\frac{(i-1)(4p-3i)}{2}. $$

Fix $W\in\mathcal{Y}$ and consider the fiber $\pi^{-1}(W)$ . Since $x$ preserves $W$ and is self-adjoint, it operates on $W$ and $W^{\perp}/W$ . The symplectic form descends to $W^{\perp}/W$ , and the action of $x$ is self-adjoint with respect to it. Let $\mathfrak{p}_{W^{\perp}/W}$ be the space of these endomorphisms. We get a map

$$ \eta:\pi^{-1}(W)\longrightarrow\mathfrak{gl}_{W}\times\mathfrak{p}_{W^{\perp}/W}. $$

Since $\dim(W^{\perp}/W)=2(p-i)$ , the base has dimension

$$ \dim\mathfrak{gl}_{W}+\dim\mathfrak{p}_{W^{\perp}/W}=i^{2}+\dim\bigwedge^{2}(W^{\perp}/W)^{*}=i^{2}+(p-i)(2(p-i)-1). $$

Fix $x_{1}\in\mathfrak{gl}_{W}$ and $x_{2}\in\mathfrak{p}_{W^{\perp}/W}$ . The image of $\eta$ consists of all such pairs for which $v$ generates $W$ under $x_{1}$ . This is an open condition on $x_{1}$ , so the image is open. Now consider a nonempty fiber $\eta^{-1}(x_{1},x_{2})$ . Let $P_{W}\subseteq\check{G}$ be the stabilizer of the flag $W\subseteq W^{\perp}$ , let $U_{W}$ be its unipotent radical, and put $\mathfrak{u}_{W}=\operatorname{Lie}(U_{W})$ . Then $\mathfrak{u}_{W}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ operates on the fiber by translation, making it a $\mathfrak{u}_{W}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ -torsor. In a symplectic decomposition $V=W\oplus E\oplus W^{*}$ , its free blocks are an arbitrary $W\otimes E$ block and an alternating $W\otimes W$ block. Thus

$$ d:=\dim(\mathfrak{u}_{W}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p})=2i(p-i)+\frac{i(i-1)}{2}. $$

Putting it all together,

$$ \displaystyle\dim\ell^{-1}(i) \displaystyle=\frac{(i-1)(4p-3i)}{2}+i^{2}+(p-i)(2(p-i)-1)+d \displaystyle=2p^{2}-3p+2i. $$

By comparison, $\dim\mathfrak{p}_{2p}=\dim\bigwedge^{2}V^{*}=2p^{2}-p$ . So the desired codimension is

$$ \operatorname{codim}_{\mathfrak{p}_{2p}}\ell^{-1}(i)=(2p^{2}-p)-(2p^{2}-3p+2i)=2(p-i), $$

which is at least two when $i<p$ . ∎

#### Corollary 3.8.7.

The complement of the open subvariety $\mathcal{U}=\ell^{-1}(p)$ in $\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ has codimension at least two.

#### Proof.

The complement $\mathfrak{p}_{2p}\setminus\mathcal{U}$ is the union of the subvarieties $\ell^{-1}(i)$ for $1\leq i<p$ , so the claim follows from Lemma 3.8.6. For $p=1$ the complement is empty. ∎

#### Lemma 3.8.8.

Every $x\in\mathcal{U}$ is conjugate under $\check{G}_{X,v_{0}}$ to an element of $(\check{\mathfrak{b}}+f)\cap\mathfrak{p}_{2p}$ .

#### Proof.

Since $x\in\mathcal{U}$ , the vectors $v_{2p}:=v_{0},v_{2p-1}:=xv_{0},\ldots,v_{p+1}:=x^{p-1}v_{0}$ span a Lagrangian subspace $W$ . By Lemma 3.8.3 and the maximality of $W$ , we have $x^{p}v_{0}\in W$ . Hence $W$ is $x$ -stable and $x$ operates on $V/W$ . The form $\omega$ induces a perfect pairing $W\times V/W\to\mathbf{C}$ . Choose a Lagrangian complement to $W$ and its basis $v_{1},\ldots,v_{p}$ such that $\omega(v_{i},v_{2p+1-j})=\delta_{ij}$ . Then there exists a unique $k\in\check{G}_{X}$ such that $k\mathbf{e}_{i}=v_{i}$ . Since $k\mathbf{e}_{2p}=v_{0}=\mathbf{e}_{2p}$ , we have $k\in\check{G}_{X,v_{0}}$ .

In this basis the lower-right block $D$ of $k^{-1}xk$ has ones on its superdiagonal and zeros above it. The upper-right block is zero because $W$ is stable. Self-adjointness makes the upper-left block $J_{p}D^{t}J_{p}$ , with the same superdiagonal pattern. All remaining entries lie on or below the diagonal. Thus $k^{-1}xk\in\check{\mathfrak{b}}+f$ . ∎

#### Corollary 3.8.9.

The image of the action map $q:\check{G}_{X}\times^{\check{U}_{X}}\mathcal{T}\to\mathfrak{p}_{2p}\times V$ is

$$ \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{cyc}}=\{(x,v):v,xv,\ldots,x^{p-1}v\text{ are linearly independent}\}. $$

The complement of its image has codimension two.

#### Proof.

The prescribed superdiagonal entries give $\operatorname{im}q\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{cyc}}$ . The reverse inclusion follows from the preceding lemma and the transitivity of $\check{G}_{X}$ on $V\setminus\{0\}$ . Over nonzero $v$ , the stratum of cyclic dimension $i$ has codimension $2(p-i)$ by Lemma 3.8.6; the locus $v=0$ has codimension $2p$ . For $p\geq 2$ , the nonempty stratum $i=p-1$ has codimension two. For $p=1$ , the complement is $\mathfrak{p}_{2p}\times\{0\}$ , again of codimension two. ∎

Putting things together, we get:

$$ \mathrm{QCoh}^{GL_{p+q}}(GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}\mathcal{N}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash} $$

be the sheared dg-category of equivariant quasi-coherent complexes on the null-cone $\chi_{\check{M}}^{-1}(0)\cong GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}\mathcal{N}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}$ . It has a natural pushforward functor to $\mathrm{QCoh}^{\check{G}}(\check{M})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash}$ .

Let $\mathrm{Perf}^{GL_{p+q}}(GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}\mathcal{N}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash}\subset\mathrm{QCoh}^{GL_{p+q}}(GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}\mathcal{N}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash}$ be the subcategory of compact objects.

#### Theorem 4.3.1.

There is an equivalence of dg categories

$$ \mathrm{Ind}(D^{b}_{\{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)\}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)}))\cong\mathrm{QCoh}^{GL_{p+q}}(GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}\mathcal{N}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash} $$

which restricts to an equivalence

on compact objects.

#### Proof.

The same proof as in [CMNO, Theorem 5.5.] or [C, Theorem 4.8] in view of Proposition 2.4.4 and the Theorem 4.1.2.

### 4.4. Abelian equivalences

Put $\delta=q-p$ , $H=\check{G}_{X}=\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}$ , $V=\mathbb{A}^{2p}$ , and $W=T^{*}V=V\oplus V^{*}$ . Consider the dg algebras with zero differential

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{A}_{p,q} \displaystyle=\operatorname{Sym}^{*}\left(\wedge^{2}V[1]\oplus(\Pi^{\delta+1}W)[\delta]\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{\delta}\mathbb{A}^{1}[2i-1]\right), \displaystyle\mathfrak{B}_{p,q} \displaystyle=\operatorname{Sym}^{*}\left(\wedge^{2}V[-2]\oplus(\Pi^{\delta+1}W)[-\delta-1]\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{\delta}\mathbb{A}^{1}[-2i]\right). $$

Write $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{p,q}$ and $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B}_{p,q}$ . Our convention is that $E[k]$ lies in cohomological degree $-k$ , and the symmetric algebras use the sign $(-1)^{ij+\epsilon\eta}$ for cohomological degrees $i,j$ and internal parities $\epsilon,\eta$ . All modules are left modules. Their internal parity is prescribed by the central element $(-I)^{\delta+1}\in H$ ; thus an independent parity shift does not give additional simple objects.

The algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ is finite-dimensional and nonpositive, while $\mathfrak{B}$ is polynomial with generators in strictly positive degrees and $\mathfrak{B}^{0}=\mathbb{C}$ . Let $D^{H}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}\mathrm{-mod})$ denote the category of equivariant dg modules with finite total cohomology, and let $D^{H}_{perf}(\mathfrak{B}\mathrm{-mod})$ be the thick subcategory generated by $\mathfrak{B}\otimes U$ for finite-dimensional $H$ -representations $U$ . Using the $H$ -equivariant self-dualities of $\wedge^{2}V$ and $W$ , Koszul duality gives

$$ \kappa:D^{H}_{perf}(\mathfrak{B}\mathrm{-mod})\xrightarrow{\sim}D^{H}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}\mathrm{-mod}),\qquad M\longmapsto\mathbb{C}\overset{\mathbf{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathfrak{B}}M, $$

where the derived fiber carries its Koszul $\mathfrak{A}$ -action; see [BFGT, Section 3.8]. Equivalently, $\kappa$ is the inverse of $N\mapsto R\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathfrak{A}}(\mathbb{C},N)$ under $\mathfrak{B}\simeq R\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak{A}}(\mathbb{C})^{\mathrm{op}}$ .

The standard $t$ -structure on $D^{H}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}\mathrm{-mod})$ is bounded, with heart the finite-dimensional $H$ -equivariant $H^{0}(\mathfrak{A})$ -modules. Hence

$$ D^{H}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}\mathrm{-mod})^{\heartsuit}\cong\begin{cases}\wedge^{*}W\mathrm{-mod}(\mathrm{Rep}(H)),&p=q,\\
\mathrm{Rep}(H),&p<q.\end{cases} $$

Recall from Theorem 4.2.1 the derived Satake equivalence

$$ \displaystyle\Phi^{b}:D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)}) \displaystyle\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Perf}^{H}\left(\wedge^{2}V[2]\times W[\delta+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}_{\delta}^{*}[2]\sslash GL_{\delta}\right) \displaystyle\xrightarrow{\sim}D^{H}_{perf}(\mathfrak{B}\mathrm{-mod}) $$

#### Theorem 4.4.1.

The composed equivalence

$$ \kappa\circ\Phi^{b}:D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\xrightarrow{\sim}D^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}_{p,q}\mathrm{-mod}) $$

is $t$ -exact for the perverse $t$ -structure on the left and the standard $t$ -structure on the right. It induces an equivalence of abelian categories

$$ \mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\cong\begin{cases}\wedge^{*}(T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p})\mathrm{-mod}(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p})),&p=q,\\
\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}),&p<q.\end{cases} $$

Here modules and representations are finite-dimensional. The same holds for $\mathfrak{L}X$ with its $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -action.

#### Proof.

Let $\lambda\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}$ be a dominant real coweight, and let $V^{\lambda}\in\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p})$ and $\mathrm{IC}^{\lambda}_{\mathbf{R}}$ be the corresponding irreducible representation and IC complex. It follows from the construction that

$$ \Phi^{b}(\mathrm{IC}^{\lambda}_{\mathbf{R}})\cong\mathfrak{B}_{p,q}\otimes V^{\lambda},\qquad\kappa(\mathfrak{B}_{p,q}\otimes V^{\lambda})\cong V^{\lambda}. $$

Hence $\kappa\circ\Phi^{b}(\mathrm{IC}^{\lambda}_{\mathbf{R}})\cong V^{\lambda}$ lies in the standard heart. According to Proposition 2.4.4(1), the simple perverse sheaves are the $\mathrm{IC}^{\lambda}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Since every object of the perverse heart has finite length, $\kappa\circ\Phi^{b}$ sends this heart into the standard heart. Both $t$ -structures are bounded, so $\kappa\circ\Phi^{b}$ is $t$ -exact and induces an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\cong D^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}_{p,q}\mathrm{-mod})^{\heartsuit}. $$

The theorem follows from the description of the heart above. The assertion for $\mathfrak{L}X$ follows from Proposition 2.4.5. ∎
